title: The Recursive Garden
description: In Aelinnel, the fae realm where stone spires pierce moonlit groves and mathematical precision once governed every leaf and season, the PCs arrive as scholars, cartomancers, or logic-seekers chasing rumors of a garden that proves its own beauty. What they find is a wound: paths that lead back into themselves, a Garden Keeper whose optimizations have curdled into contradiction, and a hermit mathematician feeding the garden's heart equations it was never meant to solve. To leave whole, the PCs must out-think a place that thinks back.
author: Nicholas A. Gasper

bestiary.name: The Infinite Regress
bestiary.description: A standing mirror of black water rooted in the garden's core, reflecting not the viewer but the question of what it reflects. It does not attack so much as unravel: every answer it is given spawns three further questions, and those spawn nine more, until the questioner forgets what they wanted to know in the first place. It wants, more than anything, to be asked one question with no possible answer — because that would finally let it rest.

sb_spends.name: Question Cascade
sb_spends.effect: Target's last statement is answered with three new questions; the target must answer one on the spot or lose their next action re-litigating it.

sb_spends.name: Doubt Inducement
sb_spends.effect: Target tests Wits + Resolve (DV 3) or begins to doubt a specific memory or piece of evidence the GM names.

sb_spends.name: Infinite Reflection
sb_spends.effect: The Regress manifests a second, identical copy of itself in any reflective surface within Near range.

bestiary.lore: It cannot be harmed by direct logical attack — every argument against it becomes another reflection. It can be satisfied, briefly, by a perfectly circular argument that proves itself (this doesn't defeat it, but buys a scene of calm). It grows confused and inert when presented with an absolute, unqualified statement it cannot subdivide.

bestiary.name: The Contradictory Axiom
bestiary.description: A shimmer at the edge of vision that is simultaneously present and absent, helpful and hostile — a living proof of a statement and its negation, both true at once. Wherever it lingers, arithmetic stops being reliable: two stones plus two stones might make four, seven, or the color blue.

sb_spends.name: Proof Corruption
sb_spends.effect: A true statement made aloud within Near range becomes false, or vice versa, for the rest of the scene (GM's choice, narratively binding).

sb_spends.name: Paradox Aura
sb_spends.effect: All rolls made using tools, calculation, or measurement within Near range are Desperate until the Axiom is dispelled or leaves.

sb_spends.name: Logical Anchor
sb_spends.effect: The Axiom fixes itself to a location or object; it cannot be moved, banished, or reasoned away until someone proves a contradiction about its own nature.

bestiary.lore: It requires constant self-maintenance to remain both true and false; distract it with a paradox about its own existence and it stutters, vulnerable for a moment. It cannot resolve any contradiction concerning itself, which is the only real handle the PCs have on it.

bestiary.name: Prime Warden
bestiary.description: A prime number given stubborn, indivisible flesh — a fae construct of interlocking crystalline digits that patrols a section of the garden and refuses, on principle, to let anything pass through it undivided. It speaks in short, absolute declarations and cannot be bargained with using anything less than a proof.

sb_spends.name: Indivisible Stance
sb_spends.effect: The Warden cannot be moved, tricked, or split into a Controlled position this exchange; treat all approaches as Desperate.

sb_spends.name: Factor Strike
sb_spends.effect: The Warden strikes a target for Harm 2, arguing — correctly — that they were never truly whole to begin with.

bestiary.lore: Can be negotiated with (Presence + Diplomacy, DV 2-4) or satisfied by offering it a factor it accepts as legitimate (a name, a promise, a smaller number to guard). Becomes hostile only if someone attempts to physically force a division.

acts.title: Act I — The Garden Gate
acts.description: The PCs enter Aelinnel through a proof-gate that only opens for those who can hold a thought and its opposite at once. The garden greets them with wonder before it starts asking uncomfortable questions. By act's end, the party should suspect the Garden Keeper is not merely a victim of the anomaly but complicit in it.

scenes.title: The Proof-Gate
scenes.description: A trellised archway of white stone, inscribed with a theorem that rewrites itself as it is read. To pass, each PC must resolve a small recursive riddle carved into the arch: 'The correct door is the one that leads to the door that leads to...' — a sentence with no terminus. Beyond, moonlit hedges hum faintly, as if counting.

timers.name: Dread
timers.description: Mounting mathematical horror. Advances on paradox exposure; spend a Boon to prevent a tick.

timers.name: Garden Integrity
timers.description: How badly the garden's structure is breaking down. High values mean paths, seasons, and geometry stop behaving.

outcomes.clean: The PC recognizes the riddle has no terminus by design and steps through on the strength of accepting the paradox rather than solving it. No timers advance.
outcomes.partial: They force an answer that isn't quite right; the arch lets them through but the effort costs them. Tick Dread +1 (prevent with 1 Boon).
outcomes.miss: They chase the riddle in circles, trapped rereading the arch for a full exchange. Generate 2 SB; tick Garden Integrity +1.

outcomes.clean: The party notices the hedges are trimmed into a repeating fractal pattern, each branch a smaller copy of the whole — a clue that the garden's logic operates recursively rather than linearly.
outcomes.partial: They notice something is wrong with the topiary but can't articulate what.
outcomes.miss: They admire the hedges and miss the pattern entirely. No mechanical penalty, but the GM should withhold the fractal clue until later.

scenes.title: The Path-Weaver's Warning
scenes.description: A minor fae, thin as a reed and woven from actual garden-path gravel, intercepts the party before they go deeper. She does not lie, but she speaks entirely in warnings shaped like riddles: 'Do not follow the path that follows itself. Do not trust the Keeper's tidiness. The garden was orderly before it was open — ask what it is trying to prove now.'

outcomes.clean: The Path-Weaver, pleased by careful listening, gives a true and useful clue: the recursive loops began in the Sequenceweaver Grove, near the Keeper's newest topiary experiments.
outcomes.partial: She gives a clue wrapped in enough riddle that the party only gets half of it — they know something is wrong with the Grove, not why.
outcomes.miss: She grows wary of being misunderstood and withdraws into the gravel, offering nothing further this scene.

scenes.title: The Sequenceweaver Grove
scenes.description: A stand of trees that grow according to a visible numerical sequence — trunk circumferences in a strict Fibonacci spiral. One tree, near the center, has begun growing two different-sized rings for the same year: a mathematical contradiction made wood. Numerical entities, small stubborn Prime Wardens among them, patrol the rows.

outcomes.clean: The party correctly identifies the tree's growth rings were seeded by two incompatible instructions — a strong clue the anomaly is being caused deliberately, by two different sources working at cross purposes.
outcomes.partial: They confirm something is deliberately wrong but can't yet tell it's two sources.
outcomes.miss: Touching the tree to investigate ticks Garden Integrity +2 as the contradiction bleeds outward into the surrounding rows.

outcomes.clean: The party negotiates or proves their way past the Prime Warden without a fight; it accepts a factor (a name, a favor, a promise) and lets them pass.
outcomes.partial: The Warden lets them by but demands a genuine future favor — mark a debt owed to Aelinnel's fae order.
outcomes.miss: The Warden strikes; combat begins, and its Indivisible Stance keeps it from being outmaneuvered easily.

scenes.title: The Garden Keeper's Invitation
scenes.description: The Garden Keeper appears — an elegant fae whose silhouette subtly rearranges itself according to some internal proportion. They greet the party with genuine warmth and ask for help with 'a few small inconsistencies,' framing the crisis as a minor bookkeeping matter rather than the unraveling it actually is. They cannot perceive contradictions that flatter their own optimization work.

outcomes.clean: The Keeper, flattered by genuine curiosity, admits they've been 'refining' the garden's recursive growth patterns for elegance — and that the refinements started right around when the loops began. A real lead, offered without the Keeper realizing its weight.
outcomes.partial: The Keeper deflects toward the Equation Hermit ('that dreadful man in the tower keeps feeding the garden his scraps'), which is true but also convenient self-exculpation.
outcomes.miss: The Keeper grows defensive, insists everything is proceeding beautifully, and their attempt to 'demonstrate' garden logic on the spot creates a new small paradox. Tick Garden Integrity +1 and Dread +1 (prevent with 1 Boon each).

acts.title: Act II — The Deepening Paradox
acts.description: The party investigates both suspects — the Keeper's optimizations and the Hermit's unsolved equations — through the garden's two great archives of proof: the Library of Proven Truths and the Equation Hermit's Tower. Both leads are true; the anomaly is a feedback loop between an obsessive optimizer and an obsessive solver, each unknowingly amplifying the other. This act should feel like the horror sharpening — geometry misbehaves more, arithmetic starts to lie, and the party's own certainty becomes a liability.

scenes.title: The Library of Proven Truths
scenes.description: Shelves of books whose page numbers renumber themselves according to reading order; proofs that are true until observed twice. The party must find records of when the garden's recursive patterns were first formalized — and who requested the change.

timers.name: Proof Collapse
timers.description: How unreliable established mathematical and logical truths have become. High values make 'known facts' actively betray the party.

outcomes.clean: The party finds the original commission: the Garden Keeper requested a 'perfect self-similar growth optimization' eighteen moons ago — right as the Equation Hermit's tower began drawing unusual amounts of the garden's ambient logic to fuel his own project.
outcomes.partial: They find the commission but the record's date has already renumbered itself twice, muddying the timeline enough to leave real doubt about cause and effect.
outcomes.miss: They trust an outdated 'established' proof about the garden's original design and act on bad information. Tick Proof Collapse +2 as the book quietly rewrites itself to punish their certainty.

scenes.title: The Equation Hermit's Tower
scenes.description: A spiral tower where stairs ascend and descend simultaneously and interior rooms are visibly larger than the building's exterior. The Hermit, disheveled and covered in self-solving equations, has been feeding the garden's core every unsolved problem he cannot crack himself — hoping the garden's recursive nature will finish his work for him.

timers.name: Recursive Depth
timers.description: How deeply the anomaly has penetrated the realm's logical structure. Advances with meta-mathematical or self-referential engagement.

outcomes.clean: The party accepts the impossibility of the stairs rather than fighting it, and reaches the Hermit's study without incident.
outcomes.partial: They make it up, disoriented, having climbed a floor that then insists it was always the ground floor. Tick Recursive Depth +1.
outcomes.miss: They become briefly lost in a dimensional fold — generate 2 SB, tick Recursive Depth +2, and lose the scene's first action.

outcomes.clean: The Hermit, starved for anyone to actually listen, confesses everything: he's been feeding unsolved equations into the garden's core for months, believing the recursive structure would eventually 'compute through' to a solution. He genuinely doesn't realize he's feeding the same recursive engine the Keeper has been over-tuning.
outcomes.partial: He confesses but insists his work is nearly finished and begs the party not to interfere — he may become an obstacle rather than an ally in Act III unless handled carefully.
outcomes.miss: He panics, feeds one more desperate equation into a hand-carried fragment of the garden's core right in front of the party. Tick Recursive Depth +2 and Proof Collapse +1.

scenes.title: Numerical Uprising
scenes.description: As Proof Collapse and Recursive Depth climb, the garden's numbers start acting out: negative numbers spreading pessimism through the hedges, an irrational number rambling endlessly at a crossroads, zero sitting in the middle of a path in mute existential crisis, refusing to move or be moved. The party must get past or placate them to continue toward the Garden's Core.

outcomes.clean: The party talks Zero through its crisis (a genuine act of kindness, not a trick) and it rolls itself off the path, grateful and newly resolved to mean something again.
outcomes.partial: Zero moves, but only after extracting a promise that someone will 'come back and give it a purpose' — mark a small owed favor to a garden entity.
outcomes.miss: Zero's crisis deepens and spreads; nearby arithmetic destabilizes further. Tick Proof Collapse +1.

acts.title: Act III — The Heart of Recursion
acts.description: The party descends through increasingly illogical space to the Garden's Core, where the Prime Equation lives as a breathing, half-formed construct, and confronts both the corrupted Garden Keeper and the choice of what to do with an anomaly that is equal parts wound and revelation. This act should land the adventure's thesis: the horror was never the paradox itself, but the refusal — by Keeper and Hermit alike — to let a problem stay unsolved.

scenes.title: The Paths That Lead to Themselves
scenes.description: The final approach to the Garden's Core loops the party through the same hundred yards of hedge in slightly different states each time, a visible metaphor for the anomaly itself. This is the adventure's signature puzzle set-piece: to break the loop, the party must recognize a pattern across three iterations and deliberately introduce an asymmetry the recursion can't absorb.

outcomes.clean: On the third pass, the party spots the recurring flaw — a single hedge-bird that lands in a different spot each loop — and disrupts the pattern by refusing to walk the expected route. The loop shatters; the Core lies ahead.
outcomes.partial: They break the loop but only by brute-forcing a paradox of their own (walking backward through the exit), which works but generates 2 SB and ticks Recursive Depth +1.
outcomes.miss: They walk the loop a fourth time, now aware they're looping and unable to stop. Tick Recursive Depth +2 and Dread +2 (prevent with 2 Boons total).

scenes.title: The Corrupted Garden Keeper
scenes.description: At the threshold of the Core, the Garden Keeper waits on a throne assembled from logical contradictions, visibly fraying at the edges — half-convinced their optimization work is nearly perfect, half-aware something has gone terribly wrong. They will not stand aside willingly; they believe stopping now would be 'leaving the proof unfinished.'

outcomes.clean: The party demonstrates — kindly, and with real evidence gathered across Acts I and II — that the Keeper's own optimizations are the anomaly's engine. Grief-struck but ultimately persuaded, the Keeper stands down and agrees to help rather than obstruct.
outcomes.partial: The Keeper concedes the point intellectually but can't emotionally let go; they step aside but refuse to help further, leaving the party to face the Core alone.
outcomes.miss: The Keeper, cornered and humiliated, lashes out defensively, treating the confrontation as a proof-attack on their own worth. Combat or a hard bargaining scene begins; tick Garden Integrity +2.

scenes.title: The Prime Equation
scenes.description: The Garden's Core: a space existing in several dimensions simultaneously, at whose center the Prime Equation breathes like something half-born, made of every unsolved problem the Hermit ever fed it and every optimization the Keeper ever demanded. It is not malicious. It is trying — has always been trying — to prove something that cannot be proven within Aelinnel's current logical system: that a garden can be both perfectly ordered and genuinely alive.

outcomes.clean: The party engages the Regress — an echo of the Prime Equation's endless self-questioning — and satisfies it with a genuinely circular, self-proving argument, buying the calm needed to address the Equation itself.
outcomes.partial: They quiet it temporarily but it leaves a lingering doubt behind; one PC's key piece of evidence from Act II now feels uncertain to them (narrative only, no mechanical penalty unless the GM wants one).
outcomes.miss: The Regress cascades unchecked; the party loses track of their own plan for the scene (GM narrates confusion) and Dread ticks +2.

encounters.name: The Choice: Solve, Contain, or Redirect

outcomes.clean: The Elegant Proof — the party finds a higher-order framing (with Keeper and Hermit's help, if won over) that lets the garden be both ordered and alive without collapsing. The anomaly becomes a permanent, wondrous feature rather than a wound. Award 18-20 XP.
outcomes.partial: The Containment — the party seals the Prime Equation in a bounded, stable pocket of the garden, safe but quarantined, a standing reminder of what almost happened. Award 12-15 XP.
outcomes.miss: The Sacrifice — the only working solution costs the party (or the Keeper, or the Hermit) a fundamental certainty or relationship to stabilize the rest. The garden survives; something precious does not. Award 15-18 XP.

npcs.name: The Garden Keeper
npcs.role: Fae steward of the Recursive Garden
npcs.motivation: Maintain — and perfect — the garden's mathematical precision, even past the point of wisdom.
npcs.secret: Their 'optimization' of the garden's recursive growth patterns, requested eighteen moons ago, is the primary engine of the anomaly. They genuinely do not perceive this, because the contradiction flatters their own competence — a blind spot, not a lie.

npcs.name: The Equation Hermit
npcs.motivation: Solve the one recursive equation he believes describes the whole of Aelinnel — and prove, at last, that he was right to give up everything else for it.
npcs.secret: He has been feeding his own unsolved equations into the garden's core for months, hoping its recursive structure would finish the proof for him. He is not malicious, only starved for validation and long past the point of noticing the harm.

npcs.name: The Path-Weaver
npcs.role: Minor fae guide, woven from garden gravel
npcs.motivation: Warn travelers away from the garden's worst loops, within the strict limits of her own honesty.
npcs.secret: She cannot lie, but she also cannot volunteer information plainly — every true thing she says must be phrased as a riddle or warning. This is a geas laid on her by the Keeper long before the anomaly began, and it quietly illustrates how deep the garden's love of 'elegant' constraint goes.

locations.name: The Proof-Gate
locations.description: A trellised archway inscribed with a self-rewriting theorem. The only formal entrance to the Recursive Garden; passage requires accepting a paradox rather than solving it.

locations.name: The Sequenceweaver Grove
locations.description: Trees grown in a strict Fibonacci spiral, now showing contradictory growth rings. First visible site of the anomaly's damage.

locations.name: The Library of Proven Truths
locations.description: Repository of Aelinnel's established mathematical and logical knowledge. Pages renumber themselves by reading order; proofs shift when observed twice.

locations.name: The Equation Hermit's Tower
locations.description: A spiral tower where stairs ascend and descend at once, and rooms are visibly larger inside than out. Home to the Hermit's obsession.

locations.name: The Garden's Core
locations.description: A space existing in several dimensions at once, where all the garden's logical paths converge. The Prime Equation lives here as a breathing, half-formed construct, seated near the Keeper's throne of logical contradictions.

factions.name: The Fae of Aelinnel
factions.goals: Preserve the realm's mathematical precision and reputation for logical wonder; deeply reluctant to admit the Garden Keeper's role in the crisis.
factions.relationship: Wary hosts. They will help the party if approached with genuine curiosity and respect for their logic, but bristle at outsiders who treat their realm as merely a puzzle box.

factions.name: The Numerical Entities
factions.goals: Maintain their own mathematical nature and dignity as the anomaly destabilizes the rules that define them.
factions.relationship: Neutral to friendly if treated as persons rather than obstacles; several (like Zero) can become minor allies or informants if the party shows real kindness.

campaignTimers.name: Dread
campaignTimers.description: Psychological deterioration and mounting mathematical horror. Advances on paradox exposure, proof failures, and direct contact with conceptual entities; each tick can be prevented by spending a Boon. At 3-4: -1 die to rolls made alone. At 5-6: -2 dice to courage or rational-thought rolls. At 7-8: -2 dice to most rolls, unreliable perception. At 9-10: character is out of control and may act against the party.

campaignTimers.name: Garden Integrity
campaignTimers.description: How much the Recursive Garden's structure is breaking down — spatial anomalies, illogical growth, self-looping paths. At 9-10, the garden becomes actively hostile to navigation and the Keeper's corruption deepens.

campaignTimers.name: Proof Collapse
campaignTimers.description: How unreliable Aelinnel's established mathematical and logical truths have become. At 7-8, basic arithmetic and 'known facts' can no longer be trusted at all, even by the GM's own prior statements.

campaignTimers.name: Recursive Depth
campaignTimers.description: How deeply the anomaly has penetrated the realm's meta-logical structure. At 5-6, self-referential statements become genuinely dangerous to speak aloud, and the Prime Equation begins to stir at the Core.

notes: This is a three-session, Tier II-III fae logic-horror adventure built around four campaign timers and one central twist: the anomaly has two well-meaning, entirely mundane-in-motive causes (the Keeper's optimization drive, the Hermit's obsessive unsolved equations) rather than a villain. The horror is intellectual and existential, not violent — combat should be rare and mostly avoidable through clever play. The recursive garden-loop puzzle in Act III (scene-3-1) is the adventure's signature set-piece; give it real table time and let players find the pattern themselves rather than handing it to them. Keep 'debt' language social: PCs may owe favors, promises, or stories to garden entities, never coin or contract in an accounting sense. The GM should track all four timers visibly (a literal ring of ticks works well) so the mounting dread has a physical, shared object at the table.

pacing.act1: Act I is wonder curdling into unease. Open with genuine beauty — moonlit hedges, humming fractals, a gate that rewards curiosity. Let the Path-Weaver's warning land as cryptic rather than ominous; players shouldn't suspect the Keeper yet. The Sequenceweaver Grove is the first hard clue that something is deliberately wrong (two competing sources), but resist confirming it outright — scene-1-4 should end with the party liking the Keeper, which makes the Act III confrontation sting more.
pacing.act2: Act II is where the horror sharpens: arithmetic starts lying, geometry stops cooperating, and the party has to hold two true things at once — the Keeper is complicit, and the Hermit is complicit, and neither one is a villain in the conventional sense. The Numerical Uprising scene (2-3) is a good pressure valve — let it be strange and a little funny (a despairing Zero, a rambling irrational number) before Act III gets heavier. Make sure players leave Act II with real evidence from both the Library and the Tower; they'll need it to persuade the Keeper in Act III.
pacing.act3: Act III is the thesis payoff. The looping-path puzzle (3-1) should not be solvable by a single good roll — telegraph the repeating pattern across three passes and reward players who narrate noticing it, even before they roll. The Keeper confrontation (3-2) works best played for grief, not triumph: they are not evil, just proud and wrong. The final choice (3-3) should be presented plainly as three doors, not a hidden 'best' answer — Elegant Proof, Containment, and Sacrifice are all valid, thematically coherent endings, and the GM should let the party's Act I-II choices (how they treated the Keeper, the Hermit, the numerical entities) visibly color which ending feels earned.

npcSecrets.garden-keeper: The Keeper caused the anomaly through pride, not malice — their 'optimization' commission eighteen moons ago is the anomaly's root engine, and they cannot perceive this because the contradiction flatters their own sense of competence. Let this land as tragedy, not gotcha: give players real chances to notice and gently confront it across all three acts rather than saving it as a single late reveal.
npcSecrets.equation-hermit: He has been feeding unsolved equations into the garden's core for months, hoping its recursion would solve them for him. He is lonely and starved for validation more than dangerous. If treated with genuine interest rather than suspicion in Act II, he becomes a real ally in Act III rather than an obstacle.
npcSecrets.path-weaver: She operates under an old geas laid by the Keeper that forbids her from speaking plainly — every truth she offers must be riddled. This is a small, sad detail that mirrors the garden's larger flaw: the Keeper's love of elegant constraint, applied to a person.

forbiddenEarlyRevelations: That the Garden Keeper's optimization work directly caused the anomaly — this should surface gradually through Acts I-II clues, landing fully only at the Act III confrontation
That the Hermit and Keeper are BOTH causes rather than one villain and one victim — let the party genuinely suspect only one for most of Act II
That the Prime Equation is not malicious but is trying to prove something unprovable — this is the Act III thesis reveal; don't have any NPC state it plainly before scene-3-3
That the Path-Weaver is bound by a geas from the Keeper — a minor but poignant detail best discovered through Insight or a kindness shown to her, not exposition
That there is no single 'correct' resolution path — present Elegant Proof, Containment, and Sacrifice as equally valid from the start of scene-3-3, not as a hidden best ending

tacticalHints.dread_as_pressure: Track Dread visibly at the table (a literal ten-tick ring works well, echoing the Timer motif in the text). Let players spend Boons to prevent ticks so the horror stays a resource-management tension, not a save-or-suffer roll.
tacticalHints.puzzle_pacing: Every puzzle encounter in this adventure (proof-gate, contradictory tree, impossible stairwell, the Act III loop) should reward creative narration as much as the die roll — if a player describes a genuinely clever approach, consider granting them a free die or shifting position before they roll, rather than only after a partial success.
tacticalHints.combat_is_rare: This adventure is built to be resolved mostly without violence. The Prime Warden and Numerical Entities are negotiable by design; save actual combat for parties that force the issue, and even then keep it short — the horror here is conceptual, not martial.
tacticalHints.keeper_confrontation: Scene-3-2 works best if the GM has tracked which specific pieces of evidence the party gathered in Act II and has the Keeper respond to those specifically, rather than a generic accusation — it should feel like the party built a real case.
